facts.fact: He has the Second Lance, which the writ from command held in reserve while the Sixth and the Ninth were sent to clear the ford, and he sat his horse at Darrow's left hand, close enough to touch, on the west bank of Harrow Ford.

He and Darrow rode knee to knee from the time they were squires holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel, kneeling shoulder to shoulder with their palms on the Oathstone while it warmed under their hands.
Darrow still has his face from the morning they were knighted, when the Grace went into him the first time: a man hearing music he had only ever been told about.
facts.evidence: a man hearing music he had only ever been told about

facts.fact: By Darrow's account he has the better seat, the better manners and the better luck with the kind of women whose fathers mattered.
facts.evidence: He had the better seat, the better manners and the better luck

facts.fact: Before the crossing he watched the far bank without smiling and told Darrow to ride wide, then wider; his mouth was open on some other word when the chaplain's bell began down the line, and he shut it and looked away.
facts.evidence: for a moment his mouth was open on some other word

facts.fact: As Darrow went under, he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank already turned and already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck, one heartbeat early by Darrow's count; when the red-handed woman turned Darrow's head to the river, the Second Lance sat its horses on the west bank in perfect order, untouched, watching.
facts.evidence: Already turned. Already climbing out. Aldric bent low over its neck.

people.did: Bent low over his horse's neck on the west bank of the Wend, the horse already turned and already climbing out, as Darrow went under midriver; by Darrow's count, one heartbeat early.
people.now: Offstage since Harrow Ford, where Darrow last saw him on the west bank as the river closed over him. Seven weeks after the Binding, with six grey cloaks and a censer on the Holloway, Darrow believes that the hand that wrote his name first on their list was that of the man who has ridden knee to knee with him since they were boys; the page has only Wren's silence and her look to say who was first.

facts.fact: He captains the Ninth Lance, sixty knights and sixty squires, and has the fastest feet in the Lowmarch, having never once cared whose father mattered.
He and Aldric Vane rode knee to knee from the time they were squires and were knighted the same morning in the same cold chapel, palms on the warming Oathstone.
Before the charge he read the clan line as fleeing something in the trees behind them, coming through the ford rather than at it, and Hollis Garrow answered that the writ said clear the ford.
Hollis told him to mount up. He looked at the carts a moment longer, then at the spears in front of them, a line he knew what to do with, left the carts for command, and mounted.
facts.evidence: Where the carts went after that was a question for whoever had put the wax on Hollis's paper

facts.fact: Halfway across the Wend the Grace went out of him in a single heartbeat, frost bloomed on his mail in midsummer, and when he planted his left foot and turned toward Tobin Marsh the knee gave with no blade and nothing touching it.
As the knee folded and he went down, he saw Aldric's horse on the west bank through the spray, already turned and climbing out, one heartbeat early.
facts.evidence: Darrow, going down, saw one thing

facts.fact: The red-handed woman dragged him by the collar of his gambeson to the east bank among the standing stones, turned his head to the river, and told him in rough Vaelish to look and remember it.
He commands the Sixth Lance, which was dressing its line a hundred yards downstream of the Ninth at Harrow Ford.
He carried the sealed writ from command ordering the Sixth and the Ninth to clear the ford with the Second in reserve, and broke its wax with his thumb without looking at it.

When Darrow pointed at the carts, old people and children behind the clan line and suggested the clans were coming through rather than at them, Hollis said they were stupid, that the writ said clear the ford, and that Darrow's head was not as fast as his feet.
She stood at the front of the clan line at Harrow Ford, knee-deep in the shallows, with her hands painted red to the wrist.
Before the lances charged she looked straight at Darrow, not at the banners or the lances, and called something across the water in her own tongue that the river took.
facts.evidence: Not at the banners, and not at the lances. At him.

facts.fact: When the Ninth fell midstream she hauled Darrow out by the collar of his gambeson and dragged him east, away from his own bank, onto the gravel among the standing stones of the far shore.
She speaks rough Vaelish as well as her own tongue; the only words she said to Darrow in it were to look at the river and remember it.

What she turned his head toward: the Wend carrying knights downstream, the Second Lance sitting its horses untouched on the west bank, and a line of still grey figures in armor under the trees of the Thornwild.

people.did: Standing waist-deep in the water over Darrow on the gravel of the far bank, her hand on his jaw, turning his head toward the Wend and telling him to look and remember.
people.now: Gone from the far bank of the Wend between one look and the next. Darrow turned back from the river and she was not there, and he has not seen her since.

quote.text: Look at it. Look. Remember it.

facts.fact: He was nineteen, the youngest of the Ninth Lance.
He sang badly and constantly.
He rode at Darrow's left in the crossing and went under his own horse in the current when the Grace left the Ninth midstream.

When Darrow came off his mare, a hand came up out of the water beyond her neck, and Darrow turned toward it to get to Tobin and cover the left; the knee went on that turn, and when Darrow came up, there was only water where the hand had been.
facts.evidence: Where the hand had been there was only brown water going by

people.did: Going under his own horse in the current of the Wend, on the second heartbeat, as the Grace went out of the Ninth midstream.
people.now: Last seen going under his own horse in the current of the Wend at Harrow Ford. Nineteen of the Ninth Lance came back from the ford; Darrow knew the names of the other forty-one and did not say them.

story_so_far.aldric-vane: He and Darrow were squires together, holding other men's horses, and were knighted on the same morning in the same cold chapel with their palms on the same warming stone. At Harrow Ford he had the Second Lance, held in reserve by the writ from command, and sat at Darrow's left hand on the west bank watching the far shore, telling him to ride wide, and then wider, with some other word left unsaid in his open mouth when the chaplain's bell cut him off. When the Grace went out of the Ninth midriver and Darrow went under, the last thing Darrow saw through the spray was Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turned, already climbing out, Aldric bent low over its neck; when the red-handed woman turned his head back to the water, the Second sat its horses in perfect order, untouched, watching. Seven weeks later, with grey cloaks on the Holloway and a list of the Faithless, Darrow thought of a man in a warm room in Calden writing a name, and heard again: Ride wide today.
story_so_far.red-handed-woman: She stood at the front of the clan line at Harrow Ford, knee-deep in the shallows with her hands painted red, and looked at Darrow and no one else before calling something across the water in her own tongue that the river took. Darrow read the line she stood in as drawn up wrong, carts and old people and children where reserves should have been, warriors looking over their shoulders into the trees, and believed the clans were not coming at the lances but through them. When the Grace went out of the Ninth midstream and the knee went, a hand closed in Darrow's collar and hauled him east, away from his own bank, onto the gravel among the standing stones; it was her. She turned his head toward the river and told him in rough Vaelish to look and remember, and when he turned back from what he had seen, she was gone.
story_so_far.tobin-marsh: He rode with the Ninth Lance at Harrow Ford, at Darrow's left, when the Sixth and the Ninth were sent to clear the ford. Halfway across, the Grace went out of the Ninth: horses stumbled, lances dipped, and Tobin went under his own horse in the current. Darrow came off his mare and turned toward him, and on that turn the knee went. Nineteen of the Ninth came back from Harrow Ford.

facts.fact: Nineteen of the Ninth came back from Harrow Ford; he made himself count them, and he knows the names of the other forty-one and does not say them.

Hearing the heralds call the Ninth faithless, he held that nobody in the Ninth had broken an oath; what he could find no place for was the bedding on the clan carts, and that he had seen it and mounted anyway.
facts.evidence: that he had seen them and mounted anyway

facts.fact: The surgeons of the Lowmarch pressed the knee, watched it slide, and sent him north, and four lay brothers carried him up the Thousand Steps on a litter, feverish, while Wren Ashdown counted the steps aloud beside him and insisted there are eleven hundred and seventeen.

The last of the road to the foot of the Steps was in a salt-cart driven by a woman the lay brothers called Rae, whom he watched because the fever had taken away his choice of what to watch, and would have watched without it; she talked to her oxen and not to her passengers, looked at his leg once the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, and told him as they lifted him that they would count him up and he should not help.
He lost his right leg above the knee at Harrow Ford.

On the road back he cursed for five days without repeating himself once: the surgeon, the river, the Crown, the clans, the oxen, the weather, the carter, Darrow, and finally himself, which was when he went quiet.
On the last cart to the foot of the Steps he started on the carter, Rae, somewhere past the second milestone, and she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather.
His answer to the Crown's proclamation, which offered the Faithless mercy at the Oathspire and leave to kneel anew, was "Kneel to that," and nobody on either cart laughed.
She was standing in the gate at the top of the Thousand Steps, small and grey-braided with her arms folded, when the litter carrying Darrow reached the top.
She drove the last cart of the road north, a salt-cart off the Holloway, its load left at the landing to make room for two knights and a leg that was not there.
She talked to her oxen the whole of the last day and to her passengers not at all, and when Hollis started on her past the second milestone she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather.
A small brass bell hangs on a cord at her belt and rings when the cart jolts; at the foot of the Steps she rang it three times, hard, and after a while a bell answered from the cloud.
She looked at Darrow's leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her.
facts.evidence: the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her

facts.fact: The first of the lay brothers coming down with the litter called her Rae, as if her name were a thing you could lean on.
facts.evidence: as if her name were a thing you could lean on

facts.fact: The one thing she said to Darrow in the whole of that day, as they lifted him: 'They'll count you up. Don't help.'
facts.evidence: They'll count you up. Don't help.

facts.fact: She walked beside Darrow's litter up the Thousand Steps counting the steps aloud, and did not stop until the top.
By her count there are eleven hundred and seventeen Steps, not a thousand, and she holds that everyone who says a thousand is wrong.
When Darrow, feverish on the litter, told her she had missed a step, she denied it and went on counting.
facts.evidence: I did not miss one. Four hundred and sixteen.

facts.fact: On the night Maelis offered Darrow the two ways off the mountain, he weighed going down to kneel again, and saw Aldric's horse on the west bank, already turning, before he asked whether he could kneel after.
facts.evidence: On the west bank, in the spray, a horse was already turning.

facts.fact: Maelis Vorne found the cord in the middle of the knee snapped rather than broken, and when he said it had held for thirty-two years she answered that it had help for twelve of them, and would not explain.
Offered the Crown's way or the Binding, he chose the Binding, an art the Crown burned the knowers of three hundred years ago, and was told he may not kneel for a long time, perhaps not ever.

quote.text: I was never much good at it anyway.

facts.fact: He kept the cot next to Darrow's through the six weeks before the Binding, mostly drunk, and offered commentary.
She read Darrow's knee with two fingers and her eyes shut and judged it not broken but undone: the cord in the middle, snapped, with no blow behind it.
When Darrow said the knee had held fine for thirty-two years, she answered that it had help for twelve of them, watched his face while she said it, and did not explain what she meant.
facts.evidence: but she watched his face while she said it

facts.fact: She refused to touch the knee for six weeks, because a Binding takes the measure of whatever it is tied to and a weak leg would give him a weak knee.

She keeps a wooden box holding a curved needle and a spool of emberthread that glows like a blown coal, an old art whose practitioners the Crown burned three hundred years ago, and she asked Darrow not to tell anyone she practices it.
She performed the Binding with her bitterleaf pipe unlit in her teeth, saying very quietly, as if to someone who wasn't there, "Time makes it possible. Proof makes it permitted."
She told Darrow he could not kneel after the Binding, not for a long time and perhaps not ever.
On the night of the Binding, when the bells rang the hour, she was somewhere in the House counting them.
